title: Is the lovers' sulk a pleasure, and on what terms?
claim: The Book of Love praises the sulk in rising terms: one of love's rewards (1109), sweeter than union (1326), beyond heaven (1323), love's very pleasure (1330). Almost every praise is hedged by a condition stated nearby. It must be measured like salt and spoils if prolonged (1302), only a small துனி is wanted (1322), yet love without any quarrel is fruit at the wrong stage (1306). It is sweet only if the embrace follows (1330, கூடி முயங்கப் பெறின்), the doubt about that sequel is its own pain (1307), and it is sweet only with one who loves (1309). 1326 puts the sulk above union, and 1330 makes its sweetness depend on union.
limits: These are speeches by characters, not a treatise; 1282, which says no sulk at all is wanted when love is full, is on Parimelazhagar's reading the woman's impatience dressed as advice. The conditions limit the praise but are never offered as a retraction of it.

title: A sulk that needs no offence
claim: In chapter 132 the man lists sulks with thinner and thinner grounds: a wreath (1313), his attempt to appease her (1319), a silent look (1320), each drawing anger (காயும்). Only 1311 states a ground, other women's eyes on him. Chapter 133 then has both speakers concede there is no fault: she says he has none, yet his tenderness can bring on a sulk (1321, இல்லை தவறவர்க்கு), and he says that though men are faultless, being kept from her arms has its own savour (1325, தவறிலர் ஆயினும்); on Parimelazhagar's reading 1305 says the same. Read together, the book detaches the sulk from wrongdoing and treats the groundless sulk of chapter 132 as a pleasure in chapter 133.
limits: Manakkudavar reads 1305's நல்லவர் as the other women, and Parimelazhagar explains 1321 by her thought that others too may receive his tenderness, so jealousy survives with its ground removed. Real offence is not absent from these chapters: 1311 names him பரத்த.

title: Can one live through separation, and why does she?
claim: Several speeches say separation cannot be survived: parting is death to his life (1124), news of his quick return is for those still alive then (1151), and on Parimelazhagar's reading 1160's 'many endure the parting and live on' is irony. 1198 turns survival into a charge: none are harder (வன்கண்) than those who live on without a kind word, the word 1156 had applied to him for announcing the parting. Yet the same speaker is later alive and gives reasons: she lives by seeing him in dreams (1213) and by longing for his return (1263), the very return 1151 dismissed. Taken together, the verses deny that she can survive, then accuse her of surviving, then name what keeps her alive.
limits: This is a dramatic sequence, not a teaching about grief. Speakers vary by commentator (Manakkudavar gives 1151 to the woman), and Parimelazhagar takes 1213 as said to reassure the friend, so its explanation may be partly for show.

title: The body testifies; who decides what it proves?
claim: In the separation chapters her body speaks before she does: slipping bangles broadcast his leaving (1157, தூற்றா), shoulders announce it (1233), the bangles knew it before she did (1277), and she has been pale seven days though he left yesterday (1278; also 1185). All parties accept this evidence, but they dispute its verdict. The town reads the pallor as news about her and never says he left her (1188); the friend reads the wasted shoulders as declaring the cruel one's cruelty (1235); and she refuses that inference, pained to hear him called cruel (1236).
limits: Speaker assignments differ (Parimelazhagar gives 1233 and 1235 to the friend, Manakkudavar to the woman), and Parimelazhagar's 'before' in 1277 depends on reading the parting as one of mind while they are still together. She herself uses கொடியார் கொடுமை of him in 1169, so her refusal in 1236 is of the charge from another's mouth.
